title: Replace Words
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every root per word versus building a trie once and walking each word to find the shortest matching root.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a dictionary of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence that has a root in the dictionary as a prefix with that root. If a word has multiple matching roots, use the SHORTEST one. Words without a matching root remain unchanged.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","dictionary (root words), sentence"],["Output","The sentence with words replaced by their shortest matching root"],["Goal","Find the shortest matching prefix efficiently, using a trie or prefix-checking"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 roots, sentence up to 10^6 characters"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Replace with the shortest matching prefix from a dictionary\"","A trie of roots lets each word be checked against all its prefixes in one walk, stopping at the first (shortest) match"],["Many roots, many words to check","Building the trie once and reusing it for every word avoids redundant work"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

For each word in the sentence, the task is to find the SHORTEST root in the dictionary that is a prefix of that word. Since a shorter match should always win over a longer one when both exist, checking prefixes from shortest to longest (via a trie walk, stopping at the first end-of-root marker) directly gives the answer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Autocorrecting Words to Their Shortest Recognized Root Form
blocks.text: Picture a spell-checker that recognizes certain short "root" words, and wants to shorten any longer word starting with a recognized root down to that root, always preferring the SHORTEST recognized root if multiple could apply. Walking through the word letter by letter and stopping as soon as a recognized root is completed gives exactly this shortest match.

blocks.caption: A trie walk through the word's letters stops at the first end-of-root marker, giving the shortest matching root

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: dictionary = ["cat", "bat", "rat"], sentence = "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
Result: "the cat was rat by the bat". "cattle" becomes "cat", "rattled" becomes "rat", "battery" becomes "bat".
5. How Should We Think?

Before checking every root in the dictionary against every word directly, notice that building a trie of all roots ONCE, then walking each word through it letter by letter, finds the shortest matching root in one pass, stopping as soon as an end-of-root marker is reached.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Building a trie from all dictionary roots takes O(total characters in dictionary) once, upfront.

Observation 2: For each word in the sentence, walking it letter by letter down the trie, stopping the MOMENT an end-of-root marker is encountered, directly gives the shortest matching root (since shorter roots are necessarily encountered before longer ones along the same path).

Observation 3: If the walk runs out of trie path before finding an end marker, or the word ends first, no root matches, and the word is left unchanged.

Observation 4: This processes each word in O(word length), independent of how many roots exist in the dictionary.

This leads to building a trie of all roots once, then for each word in the sentence, walking it through the trie and replacing it with the root found at the first end-of-root marker encountered (or leaving it unchanged if none is found).
6. Brute Force Solution
For each word, check every root in the dictionary directly to see if it is a prefix, tracking the shortest matching root found.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every root against every word directly implements the definition, guaranteed correct.
This costs O(sentence words times dictionary size times word length), unnecessary once a trie shares the dictionary structure across all word checks.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(sentence words times dictionary size times word length).
Space: O(total dictionary characters).
Limitation: a trie built once from the dictionary lets each word be checked in O(word length), independent of dictionary size.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a trie from all dictionary roots once. For each word in the sentence, walk it through the trie letter by letter; the moment an end-of-root marker is reached, that prefix is the shortest matching root, so stop and use it. If the walk exhausts the trie path or the word without finding a marker, the word has no matching root and stays unchanged.
Build the trie once. For each word, walk through the trie, returning the prefix at the first end-of-root marker found, or the original word if none is found.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for "cattle" against roots "cat", "bat", "rat"
Why This Works

Since the trie shares all roots' prefixes in a single structure, walking a word letter by letter naturally encounters SHORTER roots before longer ones along the same path (a shorter root's end marker is closer to the trie root). Stopping at the very first end marker found therefore correctly identifies the shortest matching root, without needing to compare against every possible root explicitly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total dictionary characters) to build, O(sentence length) to process, independent of dictionary size per word.
Space: O(total dictionary characters) for the trie.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Replace Words is a direct, practical application of a trie: build once from the dictionary, then answer many "shortest matching prefix" queries efficiently, one word at a time.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to stop at the FIRST end marker found, potentially finding a longer (not shortest) matching root instead.
Rebuilding the trie (or rescanning the dictionary) for every word instead of building it once upfront.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A word with no matching root at all","Left unchanged in the output."],["A word that IS itself exactly a root","Replaced with itself (the root matches immediately)."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly stating "the trie naturally encounters shorter roots before longer ones on the same path, so stopping at the first end marker gives the shortest match" clarifies the correctness argument clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "replace with the shortest matching prefix from a dictionary", think: build a trie once, walk each word, stop at the first end-of-root marker.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Checking every root per word costs O(words times roots times length); building the trie once and walking each word costs O(dictionary characters + sentence length), the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: build a trie once from the dictionary, then walk each word through it to find the shortest matching prefix.
Core Idea: stop at the FIRST end-of-root marker encountered while walking a word; that is the shortest matching root.
Time: O(words times roots times length) for the brute force, O(dictionary chars + sentence length) for the trie approach.
Most Important Observation: a trie naturally encounters shorter roots before longer ones along the same path, making "stop at the first match" correct.
Interview Difficulty: a practical, accessible trie application problem.
One line memory trick: build the trie once; stop at the first end-of-root marker while walking each word.
